statement: The staff console between a seller's request and a dealer's bid: requests, inspection, pricing, auctions and payments in one dense, dark desktop tool.
team: Product designer; the operator team's size and roles are not recorded in the files
heroCaption: The request quick view: contact and car details, comment history, price history and a condition-graded valuation in one dialog over the list.

snapshot.problem: Every car passes through staff hands: requests to qualify, inspections to review, four prices to reconcile, dealers to invite and payments to confirm, all at list volume.
snapshot.role: Product designer on the operator console: information architecture, the request pipeline, pricing, auctions, users and finance, plus the inspection report.
snapshot.result: 68 console frames and a four-page inspection report. The console names four conversion metrics but records no readings of them.

context.heading: The marketplace is run by people, and this is their desk
body: Carsparency was not self-service classifieds. Between a seller entering a car and a dealer winning it sat a staff-run pipeline: requests were qualified, cars inspected and priced, dealers invited, auctions run and payments confirmed. The back office is where that work happens.

It is the largest desktop surface in the set: 68 frames at 1,440 px behind a seven-section sidebar (Requests, Trade, Cars, Car Price, Users, Finance and Setting), plus the inspection report the operation hands to buyers.

problem.heading: Four prices, two conversations and a queue that never empties
body: A car has several prices at once: what the business is aiming for, what the seller wants, what the valuation says and what dealers bid. Someone has to see all of them to close the gap.

The reasons a price moved live in conversations: some with the dealer, some internal. And requests arrive faster than they can be opened one page at a time, so the console has to let staff act from the list.

flow.heading: From request to settled trade
body: The sidebar follows the order in which a car moves. A request enters under Requests, becomes a car under Cars, gets priced under Car Price, is sold under Trade (auctions, inventory and listings) and is paid for under Finance. Users holds the three kinds of people involved: dealers, sellers and employees.
A request's status can be changed from the list itself, to Auction, Cancel auction or Review inspection, so moving a car forward does not mean leaving the queue.

solution.heading: Act from the list, open the page only when you must
body: The quick view is the centre of the console. From any row, one dialog shows the request strip (contact, phone, car, status, reason, last editor, city, created), the comment history, the price history and a valuation for each condition grade: Like New, Good, Poor condition and Very poor.

Around it, the tables are built to be shaped by the people using them: filter and sort chips that stay visible, a column manager to show or hide columns, group operations for bulk changes, and a suggested-dealer list for each car with a live countdown to the auction's end.
bullets: Requests: list, filter, quick view, inline status change, comments

Cars and Car Price: make, model, trim, year and options; four-way pricing with history

ecosystem.heading: The console turns an inspection into something a dealer can trust
body: The back office sits in the middle of the chain. It receives what the seller declared on the web and what the inspector recorded in the field, and it sends priced cars out to dealers in Pro. Its Fair price is the same figure dealers see as Fair Market Value.

The same file holds the Advanced Inspection Report, a printable record of the car: exterior, general and interior details with verification marks, then a defects page drawn on the exploded car map that also appears in the Pro file, with signature fields for dealer and buyer.

decisions.heading: Four decisions that make the console workable
decisions.lede: Read from the frames; the file shows what was built, not the debate behind it.

items.title: A quick view instead of a page
items.why: An operator working a queue loses their place every time a row opens a new page. The quick view shows everything about a request over the list and lets its status change there.
items.tradeoff: The dialog is dense, with four panels in one view.

items.title: Show every price at once
items.why: Target, seller, fair and dealer prices usually disagree. Showing all four, with a history of who changed what, makes the negotiation visible and gives the operator the gap they are closing.
items.alternatives: A single price field, which hides the operator's judgement.

items.title: Separate what the dealer can see from what staff say to each other
items.why: Dealer comments and internal communication are kept as distinct threads. One can be shared; the other can be candid, which matters for a business that sells on transparency.

items.title: Let staff shape the table
items.why: Filters and sorts stay visible as removable chips, a column manager hides what a task does not need, and group operations act on many rows at once. The table adapts to the job rather than the job to the table.

items.title: Internal tools deserve the same design attention as the product
items.body: The console is where the business's real definition of success lives: its only metrics labels are here, not on the consumer site.

items.title: Showing four prices is a product decision
items.body: Most tools pick one number and hide the rest, which makes the operator's judgement invisible. Putting all four on screen turns pricing into a conversation with a record.

items.title: Test dense screens with data that disagrees
items.body: Every row in the file shows the same request and every price the same figure, so a console built to resolve disagreement was never drawn with any.
